item.title: Benchmarking One-Dimensional Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Methods on Quantum Hardware
item.description: arXiv:2610.40851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods encounter significant computational bottlenecks in large systems and at high Reynolds number flows due to the rapid increase in degrees of freedom, even on flagship supercomputers. As quantum computers emerge, the Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Method (QLBM) has been proposed as a quantum-native alternative for solving fluid dynamics problems. However, until recently, nearly all studies have relied on classical quantum simulators rather than real quantum hardware. This study presents a benchmark of a one-dimensional QLBM implementation executed on three different IBM Quantum hardware. We design and test a quantum circuit for the advection-diffusion equation using amplitude encoding, a Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK)-type collision operator, and a streaming step with periodic boundary conditions. Our numerical experiments evaluate transpiled two-qubit gate count, total circuit depth, runtime, and accuracy metrics including maximum absolute error ($L_\infty$ norm) and root-mean-square error (RMSE). We find that the present collision and streaming operators dominate the overall cost and become the primary scalability bottleneck on current hardware. To mitigate the prohibitive cost of full quantum state tomography on hardware-based benchmarking exercises, we introduce a sampler-based measurement strategy that reconstructs macroscopic density fields directly from computational-basis measurements. This approach substantially reduces measurement overhead while preserving the expected advection-diffusion dynamics on hardware. These results provide a quantitative assessment of QLBM performance in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) regime and identify the principal algorithmic and experimental limitations that must be addressed for QLBM to become viable for fluid dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Melvina Quartey (Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute), Lucy T. Zhang (Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute)

item.title: Machine Learning-Enabled Time-Skipping Method: Theory and Perturbation-Based Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.41152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating the time evolution of practical mechanics problems requires many time steps. This cost is further compounded by the iterative nature of implicit solvers. We present a cycle-based Machine Learning-enabled Time-skipping (MLT) method. In each cycle, several time steps are skipped, a machine learning (ML) prediction bridges the gap to initialize one solver step, and the physics-based solver then runs for several steps to correct any accumulated errors. Using the Implicit Function Theorem, we derive first-order estimates that characterize how ML prediction errors propagate. These estimates identify when errors remain bounded across cycles and guide the choice of cycle parameters, independent of model architecture. We verify these estimates on the Allen-Cahn equation and a forced variant using controlled synthetic perturbations that emulate ML errors. Wall-clock measurements confirm the theoretical speedup is realizable in practice. The MLT method provides a robust framework for accelerating time-marching in dynamic simulations.
item.dc:creator: Isaac C. Bannerman, Shaowu Pan, Lucy T. Zhang

item.title: Feature-preserving interface reconstruction using piecewise circles and cusps
item.description: arXiv:2610.41305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a geometric interface reconstruction method for Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) simulations that captures both curved interfaces and sharp features using only volume fraction data. We represent interfaces with linear facets, circular arcs, and corner facets formed by two lines or arcs joined within a single cell. We first propagate local orientation constraints through a graph and merge cells to resolve ambiguities, treating topological consistency as a first-class constraint. An optional conservative refinement improves $C^0$ continuity while preserving local volume constraints. Users can independently enable circular facets, corner facets, cell merging, and continuity refinement to balance accuracy and computational cost. In its simplest configuration, our method provides a fast local line-fitting scheme competitive with state-of-the-art PLIC methods. On standard static benchmarks, the full configuration reconstructs identifiable lines, circles, and sufficiently resolved corners to numerical precision on coarse, perturbed Cartesian meshes. On varying-curvature interfaces, it achieves third-order convergence in facet-gap error and approximately first-order convergence in curvature error. These results demonstrate global volume conservation and accurate reconstruction of curved and corner features.
item.dc:creator: Jerry Liu, Kenneth Weiss, Jin Yao

item.title: Characterization of Phase Transitions with the Annealed Importance Sampling Algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2610.41500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We We explore the use of the Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) algorithm as a numerical tool to study phase transitions and critical phenomena. By mapping physical systems such as Ising and spin-glass models directly onto Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), and extending the analysis to both synthetic and trained architectures, we use a unified RBM framework to compare the performance of AIS against standard Monte Carlo methods in regimes characterized by strong fluctuations and complex energy landscapes. The unified RBM formulation allows for massively parallel sampling, offering a scalable and precise alternative to traditional Monte Carlo methods. Building on a simple, heuristic mean-field AIS initialization derived from the weights of the network, the proposed scheme enhances sampling efficiency and accuracy across all systems considered, proving its effectiveness as a tool to detect and characterize phase transitions in discrete spin and spin-like systems. Our results show that a properly initialized AIS reliably estimates thermodynamic observables, including the partition function and magnetization, while accurately detecting both paramagnetic-ferromagnetic and paramagnetic-spin-glass phase transitions across various system sizes.
item.dc:creator: A. Prat Pou, E. Romero, J. Marti, F. Mazzanti

item.title: AMPERe: an exactly divergence-free quadrature-by-expansion evaluator for near-surface Biot--Savart and virtual-casing fields in fusion geometries
item.description: arXiv:2610.41544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate magnetic-field evaluation on and near current-carrying surfaces is a recurring computational bottleneck in magnetic-confinement fusion. As targets approach the source surface, Biot--Savart and virtual-casing kernels become singular, causing standard Gauss--Legendre and upsampled trapezoidal quadratures to lose accuracy. We introduce AMPERe, a quadrature-by-expansion (QBX) evaluator for vector magnetostatic kernels on general three-dimensional, non-axisymmetric tokamak and stellarator geometries. The method develops a spherical-harmonic QBX formulation for the vector Biot--Savart and virtual-casing (Stratton--Chu) fields and expresses the resulting magnetic field as the analytic curl of a regular-solid-harmonic vector potential. This construction yields a divergence-free discrete field at every expansion order, provides analytic derivatives, and enables an a priori separation of truncation, quadrature, and geometric errors. On the rotating-ellipse benchmark of Malhotra et al. [1], QBX maintains a relative error of 2--5 x 10^{-6} throughout the near-surface regime at distance-independent cost, whereas upsampled trapezoidal quadrature exhibits O(1) errors and requires node counts scaling as (h/d)^2. AMPERe is implemented as a header-only, performance-portable Kokkos library supporting CPU and GPU backends, with target-specific and local-correction accelerations validated against the baseline. The method is further demonstrated on realistic Wendelstein 7-X configurations, including sheet-current and virtual-casing field evaluations.
item.dc:creator: H. Betar, Y. Sarazin, V. Grandgirard, D. Zarzoso

item.title: A variational phase-field theory of cohesive fracture at finite deformation
item.description: arXiv:2610.41662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper formulates a kinematically and variationally consistent phase-field theory for cohesive fracture at finite deformation. The theory introduces an independent compliance-damage field, which accommodates both diffuse distributions and singular concentrations. The phase-field is thereby freed from the dual burden of describing crack geometry and material degradation. A rank-one additive split of the deformation gradient makes separation explicit through independent crack-strain and reference-normal fields. All fields are governed by a single principle of minimum potential energy, which consistently couples nonlinear bulk deformation, crack separation, and crack-plane rotation. One-dimensional energy comparisons show that minimization favors Dirac-type concentration of compliance damage and crack strain. Strong displacement discontinuities thus emerge naturally at a finite phase-field length without being prescribed a priori, while the phase-field remains continuous. The concentrated energy recovers the exact bulk--interface structure of a sharp-crack cohesive zone model. General objective hyperelastic bulk potentials and admissible mixed-mode cohesive laws can therefore be prescribed independently, with the nominal traction--separation law unaffected by the bulk law or phase-field length. Diffuse damage can coexist with concentrated cracks, retaining deformation modes for bulk-energy relaxation during nucleation. Two- and three-dimensional examples validate the theory across large stretches, finite rotations, and complex crack paths. Notably, the computed near-tip Cauchy stress closely matches the analytical 1/r crack-tip asymptotic solution of Long et al. (2011) outside the cohesive zone.
item.dc:creator: Ye Feng

item.title: High-fidelity simulation and reduced-order modeling of optical pumping in quantum devices
item.description: arXiv:2610.41778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatially resolved modeling of optically pumped alkali-metal vapors requires the solution of a high-dimensional nonlinear diffusive quantum master equation (DQME) coupled to state-dependent light propagation. We develop a structure-preserving computational framework for this coupled three-dimensional system in the high-pressure limit. The high-fidelity solver combines second-order finite differences, explicit pseudo-time marching, and an exponential-integrator discretization of the light-propagation equation. The scheme preserves the density-matrix trace, while a derived global pseudo-time-step restriction guarantees nonnegative, bound-preserving population updates and frozen-coefficient $1$-norm stability. In the absence of a closed-form solution for the general coupled problem, the solver is verified against complementary analytical reductions, pumping-rate asymptotics, and a light-propagation invariant, all of which are accurately recovered. Tensorized GPU implementation reduces the per-iteration cost by more than two orders of magnitude relative to a single-core CPU. For repeated parameter queries, we further construct an intrusive POD--Galerkin reduced-order model. The quadratic spin-exchange term is treated by an exact nonlinear quadratic expansion, whereas the nonpolynomial and nonlocal optical-pumping term is hyper-reduced using the discrete empirical interpolation method. At out-of-sample parameter points, the reduced model closely reproduces the full-order population and polarization fields while achieving speedup of more than \(7\times10^3\) relative to the single-core CPU full-order solver. The resulting hierarchy connects verified high-fidelity simulation with efficient reduced-order prediction for spatially resolved alkali-metal spin dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Keyu Xu, Kezheng Yan, Jinbo Hu, Yanqing Shi, Xiaorui Xu, Nan Zhao, Qian Wang

item.title: Query-Efficient Quantum Multi-Objective Optimization for Materials Configuration Search via Bayesian Weight Selection
item.description: arXiv:2610.41788v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Materials design is a multi-objective problem, and recent advances in quantum optimization make it possible to bring quantum solvers to bear on such problems. The realistic near-term win, though, is not raw quantum advantage but making an expensive, noisy quantum solver usable by spending its calls wisely. Quantum Approximate Multi-Objective Optimization (QAMOO) traces a Pareto front by solving a family of scalarized Ising problems, one per objective-weight vector, with QAOA --- but chooses those weights \emph{non-adaptively}, sampling them at random, blind to what it has already found. We recast weight selection as \emph{multi-objective Bayesian optimization}: our method, BW-QAMOO (Bayes-Weighted QAMOO), picks each next weight by expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI) under a Gaussian-process (GP) surrogate over the weight-to-objective map. On a frustrated alloy-configuration benchmark across $m\in\{3,4\}$ objectives and $n\in\{10,11,12\}$ sites, BW-QAMOO reaches the same Pareto hypervolume as QAMOO's random sampling with a median 33% fewer scalarized solves across the 90/95\% targets and 60--74\% fewer than a uniform-grid baseline), on a genuine (simulated) QAOA solver; a paired Wilcoxon test confirms the saving is significant, and the advantage grows with the objective count m as the weight simplex expands and blind sampling wastes more of the budget. This is a \emph{query-efficiency} result, and we close with the open challenges on the path to real alloy data and hardware.
item.dc:creator: Onur Boyar, Seiji Takeda, Akihiro Kosugi, Indra Priyadarsini S, Lisa Hamada, Sina Klampt

item.title: A Momentum-weighted Interface Stabilization Approach for Fluid-Structure Interaction with Strong Added-Mass Effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.42034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Partitioned fluid-structure interaction (FSI) schemes permit the reuse of optimized standalone solvers but can become unstable under strong fluid added-mass effects, particularly when structural inertia is small relative to fluid inertia. This work traces the instability to the discrepancy between the interface pressure Schur complements of the monolithic and Dirichlet- Neumann partitioned systems, as revealed by a fixed-point analysis of the linearized FSI problem. Motivated by this analysis, a momentum-weighted interface stabilization (MWIS) is proposed, in which the interface pressure block of the fluid subproblem is augmented by an operator constructed from the fluid and structural interface momentum operators. The augmentation is consistent by construction, vanishing at convergence so that the monolithic solution is recovered. A sparse diagonal approximation of the operator, derived from element metrics, limits intersolver data exchange to quantities comparable in size to standard interface coupling data while requiring minimal modifications to the standalone solvers. Numerical experiments, spanning a linear model and established nonlinear FSI benchmarks, demonstrate improved coupling robustness in regimes of strong added-mass where the standard Dirichlet-Neumann scheme diverges.
item.dc:creator: Nihar Bhardwaj Darbhamulla, Xiaoyu Mao, Aditya Narkhede, David Brown, Rajeev K. Jaiman

item.title: FLUCS: a modular GPU-native framework for fluid and plasma turbulence
item.description: arXiv:2610.40794v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present FLUCS, an open-source framework for solving systems of partial differential equations efficiently on graphics processing units (GPUs), targeting models of fluid and plasma turbulence. It comprises a set of numerical solvers specialised for a well-defined class of problems and independently developed systems that supply specific systems of equations. This allows different models to share numerical infrastructure while retaining control over their individual implementation and optimisation. The present release provides a Fourier pseudospectral solver for one-, two-, and three-dimensional periodic domains solved on a single NVIDIA GPU, with integrating-factor time integration and several time-stepping and dealiasing methods. We verify its convergence, quantify its computational costs, and demonstrate its application to three reduced models of fusion and astrophysical plasma turbulence.
item.dc:creator: T. Adkins, P. G. Ivanov

item.title: A Hybrid Message-Passing and Electric-Field Representation for Electrostatic QM/MM Embedding with Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2610.41523v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Within a hybrid quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics approach a small region of a large atomistic system is described quantum mechanically, while the rest of the system is represented by a classical force field. Despite this, the computational cost of the quantum calculation severely limits the accessible simulation and sampling time. Replacing the quantum calculation with a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on quantum reference data can greatly increase the accessible simulation time. However, the accuracy and efficiency strongly depend on the specific way in which the MLIP incorporates information about the classical (electrostatic) environment. Here, we demonstrate that existing strategies based purely on features derived from an external electric field fail to distinguish certain environments, ultimately limiting their accuracy. As a solution, we propose an extension to the equivariant TensorNet architecture that mitigates this shortcoming by incorporating classical atoms close to the quantum region into the message-passing scheme, combined with features derived from the electric field for describing the environment farther away. We show that this combination achieves higher accuracy than either approach alone.
item.dc:creator: Raphael T. Husistein, Shobhit S. Chaturvedi, Thomas Weymuth, Beatriz Piniello, S\'{e}l\`{e}ne Forget, Kresten Lindorff-Larsen, Gemma C. Solomon, Markus Reiher

item.title: Commutative Coarse-graining on the Sphere
item.description: arXiv:2610.26896v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Filtering by spatial convolution underlies coarse-graining and Large Eddy Simulation, the analysis of multiscale dynamics, and data processing across the sciences. Yet, as commonly practiced on the sphere, it violates a basic consistency requirement: commutation with differential operators, which is necessary for deriving coarse-grained dynamics and preserving the physics across lengthscales. The root of the problem is nonlocality of filtering, which compares directions in different tangent planes. The same reason underlies the Foucault pendulum's precession, and it is why the commutation failure is intrinsically geometric rather than being due to the coordinate system or numerical grid. A recently proposed generalized spherical convolution is, for a given scalar kernel, the unique linear operator commuting with the radial projection, divergence, and curl. Any consistent linear operator, be it spectral truncation, wavelet transform, diffusion, Green's-function inversion, or a machine-learned convolution, necessarily takes this form. From a simulation of an unstable jet, we demonstrate commutation to within numerical round-off, whereas common filtering that ignores curvature produces significant spurious divergence where none exists and gradient errors comparable to the gradients themselves.
item.dc:creator: Chayut Teeraratkul, Hussein Aluie

item.title: Symmetry breaking transforms strong to normal correlation and false metals to true insulators
item.description: arXiv:2512.18236v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Material scientists and condensed matter physicists have long been divided on the issue of choosing the conceptual framework for explaining why open-shell transition-metal oxides tend to be insulators, whereas otherwise successful theories such as DFT often predict them to be (false) metals. Strong correlation becomes the recommended medicine. We point out that strong correlation can be mitigated by allowing DFT to lower the energy by breaking structural, magnetic or dipolar symmetries. Such local motifs are observed experimentally by local probes beyond the 'average structure' determined by X-Ray diffraction. Observed broken symmetries can arise from slow fluctuations that persist over the observation time or longer. The surprising fact is that when symmetry breaking motifs are used as input to electronic structure calculations, false metals are converted into real insulators without the recommended medicine of strong correlation. Consistently, DFT calculations that show energy lowering symmetry breaking correct most cases where DFT, even with advanced exchange-correlation functionals, previously missed the correct metal vs insulator designation. Total energy calculations distinguish systems that support energy-lowering symmetry breaking from those that do not. This approach distinguishes between paramagnetic insulating and metallic phases and shows mass enhancement in Mott metals. The reason is that symmetry breaking removes many of the degeneracies that exist in a symmetry-unbroken system, reducing significantly the need for strong correlation. If one chooses to ignore symmetry breaking, the persistent degeneracies often call for strong correlation treatment. Thus, symmetry breaking transforms strong to normal correlation and false metals to true insulators. This view sheds light on the historic controversy between Mott and Slater that still reverberates today.
item.dc:creator: Alex Zunger, Jia-Xin Xiong, John P. Perdew

item.title: Proof-Carrying Materials: Falsifiable Safety Certificates for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2603.12183v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are deployed for high-throughput materials screening without formal reliability guarantees. We show that a single MLIP used as a stability filter misses 93% of density functional theory (DFT)-stable materials (recall 0.07) on a 25,000-material benchmark. Proof-Carrying Materials (PCM) closes this gap through three stages: adversarial falsification across compositional space, bootstrap envelope refinement with 95% confidence intervals, and Lean 4 formal certification. Auditing CHGNet, TensorNet and MACE reveals architecture-specific blind spots with near-zero pairwise error correlations (r <= 0.13; n = 5,000), confirmed by independent Quantum ESPRESSO validation (20/20 converged; median DFT/CHGNet force ratio 12x). A risk model trained on PCM-discovered features predicts failures on unseen materials (AUC-ROC = 0.938 +/- 0.004) and transfers across architectures (cross-MLIP AUC-ROC ~ 0.70; feature importance r = 0.877). In a thermoelectric screening case study, PCM-audited protocols discover 62 additional stable materials missed by single-MLIP screening - a 25% improvement in discovery yield.
item.dc:creator: Abhinaba Basu, Pavan Chakraborty

item.title: FermiLink: An Agent Harness for Multidomain Scientific Simulations
item.description: arXiv:2604.03460v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) agent harnesses have been developed for autonomous scientific simulations, but most current agent harnesses are tested on single or a small set of software packages. Herein, FermiLink, an extensible open-source agent harness is introduced for multidomain scientific simulations. Its key design principle is the separation of package knowledge bases from simulation workflows, so that simulation workflows in FermiLink, from figure-level simulations to full-paper-level research on high-performance computing clusters, operate uniformly among supported packages via a four-layer progressive disclosure mechanism. This agent harness is specifically optimized for high performance computing (HPC) clusters, enabling multi-day multi-step scientific simulations in the absence of human intervention. Using OpenAI Codex as the agent provider, the capabilities of FermiLink are demonstrated across approximately 50 scientific software packages spanning nine research domains from chemistry to engineering. Systematic benchmarks on 132 real-world figure-level reproduction tasks with 44 packages show that FermiLink reproduces 74 (56.1%) of published figures with simulations, among which 30 (22.7%) achieve high-fidelity agreement and 35 reach qualitative agreement with the target figures. A smaller set of human expert-guided reproduction benchmarks with 10 packages in physics and chemistry further highlights the importance of expert insights for improving the simulation fidelity. Beyond reproduction, a single-blinded study demonstrates that FermiLink can produce research-grade results on unpublished polariton physics problems when provided with sufficiently detailed research objectives. Overall, FermiLink provides a scalable research infrastructure that may accelerate the path from scientific questions to computational results across diverse domains.
item.dc:creator: Gang Meng, Andres Felipe Bocanegra Vargas, Xinwei Ji, Federico Garcia-Gaitan, Felipe Reyes-Osorio, Jalil Varela-Manjarres, Yafei Ren, Mohammadhasan Dinpajooh, Branislav K. Nikoli\'c, Tao E. Li

item.title: A Theory-guided Weighted $L^2$ Loss for solving the BGK model via Physics-informed neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2604.04971v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While Physics-Informed Neural Networks offer a promising framework for solving partial differential equations, the standard $L^2$ loss formulation is fundamentally insufficient when applied to the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) model. Specifically, simply minimizing the standard loss does not guarantee accurate predictions of the macroscopic moments, causing the approximate solutions to fail in capturing the true physical solution. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a velocity-weighted $L^2$ loss function designed to effectively penalize errors in the high-velocity regions. By establishing a stability estimate for the proposed approach, we shows that minimizing the proposed weighted loss guarantees the convergence of the approximate solution. Also, numerical experiments demonstrate that employing this weighted PINN loss leads to superior accuracy and robustness across various benchmarks compared to the standard approach.
item.dc:creator: Gyounghun Ko, Sung-Jun Son, Seung Yeon Cho, Myeong-Su Lee

item.title: Chiral vibrational modes and vibrational circular dichroism
item.description: arXiv:2607.22257v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The recent interest in chiral phonons in a variety of physical phenomena and their hypothesized role in the chiral-induced spin selectivity effect [Phys. Rev. Research, 5, L022039 (2023)] call for further investigation into the chirality of molecular vibrations. Although molecular chirality has conventionally been quantified using structural properties, recent work has highlighted the role of dynamical response properties as chirality metrics. In this work, we examine an inter-atom helicity pseudoscalar as a complementary measure of vibrational chirality, associated with the vibrational circular dichroism (VCD) intensity in the fixed partial charge (FPC) approximation. This pseudoscalar is translationally and rotationally invariant, can distinguish between opposite enantiomers, and unlike an atomic pseudoscalar measure considered in our earlier work [Phys. Rev. Lett., 133, 268001 (2024)] does not rely on a predefined symmetry axis. For a twisted ethane model as well as several small molecules, this pseudoscalar correlates well with structural descriptors based on the continuous chirality measure. Overall, our results support response-based metrics as a physically meaningful and practically useful characterization of vibrational chirality. Importantly, while the FPC-based VCD estimate provides a useful quantifier of vibrational chirality, we show that it is a rather poor predictor of the actual molecular VCD response because the latter is strongly influenced by the (vibrational configuration-dependent) molecular electronic response.
item.dc:creator: Xuecheng Tao, Cl\`audia Climent, Ethan Abraham, Jichen Feng, Abraham Nitzan

item.title: PASS: Perturbation augmented space group structure sampling for transferable Fe-O machine learning interatomic potential
item.description: arXiv:2607.28000v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Iron (Fe) oxidation is a fundamental phenomenon that is scientifically vital and technologically significant. Despite substantial experimental efforts, accurate atomistic modelling of Fe oxidation remains elusive, which requires a reliable interatomic potential, whose development hinges on a representative first-principles training dataset. However, Fe-oxygen (O) system is known for its structural complexity, rendering the generation of high-quality first-principles dataset challenging. In this work, we propose the Perturbation Augmented Space group structure Sampling (PASS) method to generate extensive dataset for Fe-O system consisting of small-cell structures (no more than 10 atoms). Based on atomic cluster expansion (ACE) framework, we present a systematic approach to developing a transferable machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP). The accuracy and capability of the ACE potential are thoroughly validated across pure Fe and Fe-O systems through bulk, surface, and interface properties. The large-scale Fe oxidation simulations with the ACE potential capture key features of the oxidation process, including the formation of an FeO-like structure consistent with recent experimental observations. This work demonstrates that the PASS method yields an accurate and transferable MLIP that can capture the reactive complexity of oxide growth while remaining computationally practical for extended systems.
item.dc:creator: Zixiong Wei, Fei Shuang, Poulumi Dey

item.title: When more data become less informative: Finite-precision periodicization and collapse of forecast-error Lyapunov estimates
item.description: arXiv:2608.16120v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Equation-free forecast-error analysis is useful when governing equations, Jacobians, tangent dynamics, or full state vectors are unavailable and only scalar time series are observed. In this setting, the multi-horizon forecast-error curve can provide both an instability estimate and nonlinear predictive features, making its numerical reliability important. We show that long finite-precision chaotic records can enter an information-saturation regime in which increasing record length N (the total number of analyzed samples) adds repeated histories rather than new dynamical information. For the float32 logistic map, exact recurrence progressively fills the training catalogue with duplicate histories and identical futures, suppressing forecast-error growth and driving the estimated Lyapunov slope toward zero. Across 10,000 initial conditions, exact recurrence occurred by iteration 7612; across 28 stratified seeds, collapse onset strongly followed the recurrence-occupancy scale. A two-dimensional H\'enon-map control confirms that recurrence and estimator failure are separate events: the float32 trajectory enters an exact machine-state cycle after a transient of $\mu = 103,039$ samples, with cycle period P = 12,268, yet the forecast-error estimate remains close to the positive Jacobian/QR reference until catalogue saturation near N = 200,000. Casting an already generated float32 record to float64 does not restore lost information, whereas genuine float64 generation, restarted short trajectories, and one-ULP perturbations prevent collapse over the tested range. A recursive local-linear predictor exhibits the same endpoint at a later, predictor-dependent threshold. The results identify a recurrence-to-catalogue-saturation failure mode specific to forecast-error/analogue inference rather than Lyapunov estimation in general.
item.dc:creator: Andrei Velichko, Viet-Thanh Pham

item.title: Suzuki-Trotter Decompositions and other Methods for Quantum Time Evolution
item.description: arXiv:2609.19184v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: (Suzuki-)Trotter decompositions, splitting methods, (Lie) product formulae... The most common numerical methods for the time evolution of quantum systems come with many names. And they are used practically everywhere with applications ranging from the solution of classical equations of motion and various Monte Carlo simulations to the real and imaginary time evolution on classical as well as quantum computers. Here we review the state of the art of said methods, focussing especially on the progress made over the last few years. We highlight recently discovered efficient time evolution algorithms and explain how best to use them in practice. A central part of this work is the estimation of error bounds that has improved greatly within the past decade. The relevance of time evolution methods for quantum computing is discussed with a focus on noisy hardware. Finally, a comprehensive overview of generalisations, related methods and alternatives to Trotterization is provided. This includes time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, processed methods, multi-product formulae, symplectic integrators, TDVP for tensor networks, quantum signal processing, Crouch-Grossman methods and more. The overall perspective in this work is that of a theoretical physicist. All mathematical proofs as well as some technical details are omitted for easier readability. Instead, this review serves as a hands-on guide and, of course, as a starting point for references that provide further details.
item.dc:creator: Johann Ostmeyer
